newsitem.title: UK: Dlr recovers ground in Europe as EMU tensions ease.
newsitem.headline: Dlr recovers ground in Europe as EMU tensions ease.

text.p: The dollar rose more than a pfennig against the German mark in Europe on Tuesday, reversing a chunk of Monday's mark rally as tensions surrounding preparations for Europe's single currency eased a touch.
German, French and other senior politicians helped take the heated single currency debate off the boil by repeating their intention to start the project on time in 1999.

Monday's demand from the new French government for more time to consider the post-EMU budgetary stability pact has shifted the market focus to the European Union summit in Amsterdam next week. For now, the markets are betting a solution will be found.

"We're all really just waiting here. This has turned into a big puzzle and people want to see the outcome of the summit before making any long-term changes to strategies," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago.
French President Jacques Chirac today reaffirmed the government's committment to a punctual EMU start and said he hoped for a deal on the stability pact in Amsterdam summit.
Luxembourg prime minister Jean-Claude Juncker said he hopes the EU will find a solution to the impasse by the end of June.
At 1525 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.7190/00, up from 1.7055/60 late in Europe on Monday.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said French premier Lional Jospin has expressed a clear will to proceed with EMU.

Traders said the absence of the major economic data from the U.S. or Europe today added to the sense of drift, while an underlying bid for marks on its European cross rates earlier in the session was also reversed again by short-term players later in the day.

"We've seen some of the bigger accounts looking to avoid the markets altogether until this issue is cleared up," said one FX salesman at a UK bank. "People still basically think this will blow over but there is a growing demand for insurance."

The Amsterdam summit is held next Monday and Tuesday. Spanish foreign minister Abel Matutes said a second summit after the Amsterdam meeting would not be a problem if that's what it took to agree to the review of the Maastricht Treaty.

"It's going to be a crucial month for the whole EMU process," said Knuthsen at First Chicago. "The new French government has made its move and there is a risk they may have pushed the Germans just too far. We shall see."
Elsewhere, the dollar was slightly lower against the yen amid concerns the April Japanese current account data, due out at 2350 GMT tonight, will show another large surplus.
Analysts polled by Reuters expect the current account to show a surplus of 1.1 trillion yen compared with a previous 1.0 trillion yen.

U.S. Trade Representaive Charlene Barshefsky, whose comments helped trigger dollar/yen's slide late Friday and on Monday, kept the pressure on Japan not to allow its trade surpluses with the U.S. to balloon again.
Barshefsky said the U.S. does not want to see a big rise in Japan's surplus and that currency swings and higher Japanese taxes had given rise to disturbing trade trends.
